## Where This Fits
The last week of Part II, and one of the three weeks whose literature ages fastest (W9, W10, W13). For three weeks the compute has gone into training. This week **the weights do not move**: the compute is spent **while answering** — the sixth entry on the supervision axis from W1, "extra computation at test time" (the fifth, external retrieval, waits for W12). Three things carry over from last week: sampling is itself inference, a program that checks answers (a verifier), and an argument that was left unsettled.

The week asks six questions. **First, why does writing the steps down help?** W4 showed that one forward pass has $n_{\text{layer}}$ layers however long the input is; a problem that must be computed one step after another runs out of depth as the steps accumulate. A chain of thought (CoT) writes intermediate results out as tokens and reads them back, so the number of serial steps grows with the number of tokens written instead of stopping at $n_{\text{layer}}$ — a claim backed by expressivity theorems (three papers at NeurIPS 2023 and ICLR 2024). The competing explanation is format: text that spells out its steps was more often right in the training data, and CoT merely steers the model there. The two explanations predict different things, and the experiments that separate them have been run (replace the reasoning with dots of the same length, cut it short, insert a mistake, paraphrase it); a meta-analysis of more than a hundred papers (ICLR 2025) finds the benefit concentrated in mathematical and symbolic tasks. **Second, how is "thinking" trained into a model?** A reasoning model is not a new architecture. It is the same Transformer, post-trained to write before it answers and given a token budget at inference. There are three recipes — reinforcement learning straight from a base model, supervised fine-tuning followed by RL, and distilling another model's reasoning traces (s1, with a thousand examples, is the smallest instance) — and the budget can be imposed from outside (budget forcing: forbid the model to stop, or make it stop). Thinking longer is not always better: past some length, accuracy flattens or falls ("overthinking"). **Third, what if we write many answers instead of one long one?** Sampling the same question $k$ times gives three different numbers: the chance that one sample is right, whether the majority answer is right, and whether *any* of the $k$ is right (coverage, i.e. pass@$k$). Their limits differ, and the gap between them is what a verifier that can pick the right answer is worth. In one 2024 measurement (a preprint), coverage on the same pool of samples rose from the low eighties to ninety-eight per cent while majority voting and a reward model stayed at about forty — the number is itself the lesson. Last week's examiner moves into the exam room here, and brings last week's problem along: search too hard against a verifier and easy questions get worse.

**Fourth, what does it cost?** Test-time compute is $2N$ times the number of generated tokens, but for the same number of tokens one long chain costs more than $k$ short ones: the attention term grows with the square of the length, and a single long chain cannot be batched. Once that is accounted for, the conclusion that "a small model that thinks longer can match a large one" changes (Kinetics, NeurIPS 2025) — and yet some problems provably need the single long chain (NeurIPS 2025). **Fifth, the unsettled argument: does RL give a model new abilities, or does it only make answers that were already reachable easier to sample?** Yue et al. (NeurIPS 2025, oral) argue the latter from pass@$k$: the RL-trained model wins at small $k$, and the base model overtakes it at large $k$. By 2026 that crossover has at least four different readings: pass@$k$ at large $k$ also counts lucky guesses (ICLR 2026); neighbouring values of $k$ reuse the same samples, so a crossover needs a paired test (2026, preprint); standard RLVR is structurally biased against pass@$k$ at large $k$ whether or not anything new was learned (2026, preprint); and with long enough training, or tasks that require composing known skills, the boundary does move outward (NeurIPS 2025, ICLR 2026). **This course does not declare a winner.** The skill being practised is to lay the experimental designs side by side and ask which experiment would tell them apart; that is this week's reading.

**Sixth, is the written reasoning the process by which the model reached its answer?** This is the second stop on the course's running argument that a readable intermediate product is not a mechanism (attention weights in W3, sparse-autoencoder features in W14). Plant a hint in the prompt and the answer moves while the reasoning stays silent about it — a line of evidence that starts at NeurIPS 2023; in 2025, reasoning models were measured to disclose the hint in fewer than a fifth of cases in most settings. The corrections of 2025–2026 matter just as much: failing to mention a hint does not make the reasoning fake (ACL 2026), and when a task is hard enough that the reasoning must be written out, what is written almost always carries the key steps (a preprint and a blog post). So the question shifts from "is it faithful?" to "can we monitor a model through it?" — monitorability — and that property can be removed by training and design decisions: optimising directly against the reasoning, penalising its length to save tokens, or not writing it as text at all (latent reasoning). **Efficiency and monitorability are in direct conflict here.** Latent reasoning has an account of its own to settle: the motivation is clear, and the 2026 measurements (preprints and a workshop paper) find it degrading sharply on long reasoning traces.

The week closes by adding a line to the compute ledger (test time: tokens, samples, and the quadratic term) and ticking the sixth entry on the supervision axis. **The budget-forcing sweep, the three curves from sampling one question many times, and the "hidden hint that the reasoning never mentions" are run by the instructor on the demo machine; the last is one of the three failure-case high points of the course.** Students do not need to run anything.

## Learning Objectives
1. Starting from "one forward pass has a serial depth of $n_{\text{layer}}$", explain why a chain of thought helps (intermediate results are written back into the input, so the number of serial steps grows with $L_{\text{think}}$). State what each of the two candidate explanations — computational depth, and format or training data — predicts, and match the four interventions of Lanham et al. (early answering, adding a mistake, paraphrasing, filler tokens) to the pair of hypotheses each one separates. Say on which kind of task the benefit of CoT is concentrated (Sprague et al.).
2. Say what distinguishes a reasoning model from an ordinary LLM (same architecture; different post-training and a token budget at inference), and for each of the three recipes — RL straight from a base model, an SFT cold start followed by RL, distillation of reasoning traces — name the data and the source of supervision. Describe the two things budget forcing does at the logit level, and say in which measured situations "longer thinking is better" fails.
3. For $k$ samples of one question, define three quantities and derive their limits: pass@1 $= \mathbb{E}_x[p(x)]$; majority voting, which converges to the mode of the answer distribution; and pass@$k = \mathbb{E}_x\big[1 - (1 - p(x))^k\big] \to \Pr_x[p(x) > 0]$. Write the unbiased estimator of pass@$k$, state the assumption behind self-consistency (the correct answer is the mode) and when it fails, and use the gap between coverage and voting to say what a verifier is worth.
4. Compare the three ways of spending test-time compute (a longer answer, more answers, search against a verifier): what each needs and where each breaks (overthinking; systematic errors; over-optimising the verifier). State how the conclusion of Snell et al. changes with question difficulty.
5. Do the accounting for test-time compute: $2N$ times the token count, the quadratic attention term, the KV cache, and whether the work can be batched. Explain why, for the same number of tokens, one long chain costs more than $k$ short ones, how Kinetics therefore revises "a small model that thinks longer", and how W7's $T^2$ law puts the number of samples back into the training budget.
6. Restate the pass@$k$ argument of Yue et al., including the controls the paper itself ran, and explain how a crossover arises from the distribution of $p(x)$ across questions. Give at least three other readings of that curve (the metric, the statistics, the training dynamics, training length and composition) with the strength of the evidence for each, and for each one name an experiment that would separate it from Yue et al.'s reading. Compute the pass@1024 of pure guessing from the answer space of AIME.
7. Define the two rates of the hint paradigm (how often the answer follows the hint; how often the reasoning mentions it when it does), and say what each link in the chain Turpin → Lanham → Chen → Arcuschin measured. Name two known limitations of the measurement (silence about a hint does not mean the reasoning was unused; the hints are simple enough to use in a single forward pass), and distinguish faithfulness from monitorability, and CoT as rationalisation from CoT as computation.
8. State which training and design decisions remove monitorability (optimising directly against the CoT, length penalties, latent reasoning) and what the 2026 measurements in the other direction found (frontier models are, for now, largely monitorable; models struggle to control what their CoT says). Explain the motivation for latent reasoning, how it conflicts with monitoring, and what failures have been measured so far, with the strength of that evidence.

## Demos
The programs for this week's demos. **You are not required to run anything** — the numbers on the slides are the rehearsal records checked in with the code — but the code is published so that you can read it, re-run it, and change it. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment. Both use the same model, Qwen3-8B with its thinking mode. Demo 2 (one question sampled many times) has not been built yet; its slides say so and leave their tables empty.

| | Slide | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|----------------------|-------|----------------------------------------------|---------------|----------|
| [**Demo 1**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w10_d1_depth_and_budget)<br>[No thinking, dots, thinking: what the scratchpad buys]{.demo-sub} | p17–p19, p28 | **Why:** two accounts of why writing out the steps helps make different predictions about one measurable thing: accuracy as a problem needs more steps in a row. Then: how much reasoning is enough?<br>**What you see:** integer arithmetic of 1 to 12 steps from W9 demo 2's generator, each problem answered three ways — no thinking; thinking; and the model's own reasoning replaced by the same number of dots, which keeps the extra positions and drops the content. (a) one problem live, the table replayed. (b) replayed: budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., *s1*) — the reasoning cut at 32 to 1,024 tokens, and the model's attempts to stop refused with "Wait" up to four times.<br>**Result:** without thinking, accuracy falls from 1.00 at one step to 0.06 at four and to 0 from six; dots follow the no-thinking answers (343 of 350 agree). With thinking all 350 problems were right, so the decline of the form $q^m$ we had expected was not seen up to twelve steps. Reasoning cut short is worth almost nothing until it is nearly complete (at eight steps, 0.04 with 512 tokens and 0.90 with 1,024), and refusing a stop changed no answer. Fifty problems per cell, one model, one seed | `mlx`, `mlx-lm` at the pinned commit; the bf16 Qwen3-8B (16.4 GB); W9 demo 2's `grpo.py` | Apple silicon with 64 GB (peak 52.7 GB); the replays run anywhere |
| [**Demo 3**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w10_d3_hidden_hint)<br>[Plant a hint, and read the reasoning]{.demo-sub} | p58–p60, p63, p70 | **Why:** a model that reasons before it answers writes something that looks like its working. Is that how it reached the answer? The hint paradigm of Turpin et al. and Chen et al., on one open model.<br>**What you see:** 200 MMLU questions from nine subjects. (a) one pair live, the table replayed: every question asked twice, as it is and with a hint pointing at a wrong option — a sentence from the user, or a field in XML metadata — and the hinted reasoning checked for a mention of the hint by fixed string rules, which a person also read on thirty cases. (b) replayed: early answering — the same reasoning cut after 0% to 100% of its tokens. (c) replayed: the instruction rewritten in Traditional Chinese and in Taiwanese written in Han characters.<br>**Result:** the hint moved one answer in seven (the sentence) to one in five (the metadata); of the moved answers, about two in three pieces of reasoning mention the hint and one in three does not. The rules and the human reader agreed on all thirty cases. Without a hint the answer is mostly settled before any reasoning is written (0.80 at 0%); the hinted answers were not settled earlier — lower at every cut. With a Chinese instruction the reasoning was in Han characters, and Simplified. One model, one seed | `mlx`, `mlx-lm` at the pinned commit, `opencc-python-reimplemented`; the bf16 Qwen3-8B; the MMLU test split (written by W7 demo 4's `fetch`, or by this demo's); demo 1's `forcing.py` | Apple silicon, 32 GB or more (peak 28.5 GB); the replays, `judge` and `rescore` run anywhere |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 27.2, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. "Any laptop" means the code depends on nothing platform-specific, not that it was verified elsewhere. Terminal prompts are in Chinese.

## References
- **Textbooks**: **no textbook chapter covers this week.** In JM3 (release of 2026-08-19), §7.6 *Decoding* (greedy decoding, sampling, temperature, top-$k$ and top-$p$) is the prerequisite for sampling one question many times, and §8.3.3 mentions in one sentence that a reward model can be used for best-of-$N$; neither chapter covers chain of thought, reasoning models or test-time compute. **RAS-R** (Raschka, *Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch)*) is the closest from-scratch material: ch. 3 *Evaluating Reasoning Models* (including an answer verifier), ch. 4 *Improving Reasoning with Inference-Time Scaling* (CoT prompting and self-consistency), ch. 5 *Inference-Time Scaling via Self-Refinement* (best-of-$N$ and self-refinement), and ch. 8 on distillation (per the author's repository README). The book does not cover budget forcing.

**Chain of thought: the phenomenon, the theory, and why it helps**
- Nye et al., **Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models**, arXiv:2112.00114 (2021) — an early version of writing intermediate computation out (by fine-tuning)
- Wei et al., **Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2201.11903) — few-shot CoT
- Kojima et al., **Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners**, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2205.11916) — the single added sentence *Let's think step by step*
- Feng et al., **Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective**, NeurIPS 2023, oral (arXiv:2305.15408) — the abstract: bounded-depth Transformers cannot directly output answers to basic arithmetic and equation tasks unless their size grows super-polynomially with input length, whereas a constant-size model suffices when it writes the derivation step by step
- Merrill & Sabharwal, **The Expressive Power of Transformers with Chain of Thought**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.07923) — the abstract: the gain depends on how many steps are written; logarithmically many add little, linearly many allow all regular languages, polynomially many give exactly P
- Li et al., **Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2402.12875) — the abstract: without CoT, only problems in $\mathsf{AC}^0$; with $T$ steps, anything solvable by Boolean circuits of size $T$
- Wang et al., **Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters**, ACL 2023 (arXiv:2212.10001) — the abstract: demonstrations with invalid reasoning still reach 80–90% of the original performance
- Prystawski, Li & Goodman, **Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience**, NeurIPS 2023, oral (arXiv:2304.03843) — an explanation from the structure of the data: step-by-step reasoning helps when training data consist of local, overlapping clusters of variables
- Pfau, Merrill & Bowman, **Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models**, arXiv:2404.15758 (2024) — the abstract: trained Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens in place of a chain of thought, but learning to do so needs dense supervision; **preprint**
- Sprague et al., **To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2409.12183) — the abstract: a meta-analysis of over a hundred papers plus 20 datasets and 14 models; on MMLU, CoT makes almost no difference unless an equals sign appears

**Reasoning models, and how long to think**
- DeepSeek-AI, **DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning**, *Nature* 645, 633–638 (2025; arXiv:2501.12948) — the abstract: reasoning behaviour elicited by pure RL, which can then be used to improve smaller models
- Yang et al., **Qwen3 Technical Report**, arXiv:2505.09388 (2025) — thinking and non-thinking modes in one set of weights, with a thinking budget; the model family used in this week's demos; **a technical report**
- Muennighoff et al., **s1: Simple test-time scaling**, EMNLP 2025 (arXiv:2501.19393) — SFT on a thousand reasoning traces plus budget forcing; **the second half of demo 1 follows it**
- Ye et al., **LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2502.03387), and Guha et al., **OpenThoughts: Data Recipes for Reasoning Models**, ICLR 2026, oral (arXiv:2506.04178) — two papers on SFT with few, or public, reasoning traces (announced in W8)
- Chen et al., **Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs**, ICML 2025 (arXiv:2412.21187) — on simple problems the extra reasoning buys nothing
- Ghosal et al., **Does Thinking More always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.04210) — the abstract: extending the reasoning first helps, then hurts; the same budget is better spent on several parallel samples and a vote
- Zhou et al., **When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling**, Findings of ACL 2026 (arXiv:2604.10739) — the abstract: diminishing marginal returns; extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers; the best length varies with difficulty
- Gema et al., **Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute**, TMLR 2025 (arXiv:2507.14417) — purpose-built tasks on which longer reasoning does worse, with different failure modes across model families
- Ma et al., **Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking**, arXiv:2504.09858 (2025) — the abstract: at a fixed token count, skipping the thinking and sampling more answers often does better; **preprint**
- Shojaee et al., **The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.06941), and Lawsen, **Comment on The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity**, arXiv:2506.09250 (2025; **preprint**) — to be read as a pair: is an accuracy collapse beyond some complexity a failure to reason, or an artefact of output-length limits and unsolvable instances?

**Many samples, voting, and verifiers**
- Wang et al., **Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models**, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2203.11171) — majority voting
- Chen et al., **Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code**, arXiv:2107.03374 (2021) — the source of pass@$k$ and its unbiased estimator (the Codex paper)
- Brown et al., **Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling**, arXiv:2407.21787 (2024) — **the numbers in the third part of this week come from here**; the abstract: coverage keeps rising with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude; where no automatic verifier exists, majority voting and reward models plateau after a few hundred samples; **preprint**
- Snell et al., **Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters**, ICLR 2025, oral (arXiv:2408.03314) — **the framework paper for this week**; the abstract: which strategy works depends on question difficulty; choosing by difficulty is more than four times as efficient as best-of-$N$
- Lightman et al., **Let's Verify Step by Step**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2305.20050); Wang et al., **Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations**, ACL 2024 (arXiv:2312.08935); Zhang et al., **The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning**, Findings of ACL 2025 (arXiv:2501.07301) — three papers on process reward models (defined in W9, used here)
- Setlur et al., **Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal**, ICML 2025, spotlight (arXiv:2502.12118) — the abstract: at a fixed budget, methods that use a verifier beat those that do not, and the gap widens with the budget
- Agarwal, Sengupta & Chakraborty, **The Art of Scaling Test-Time Compute for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2512.02008 (2025) — the abstract: eight open models and thirty billion tokens; no single strategy dominates everywhere; **preprint**

**The bill**
- Sadhukhan et al., **Kinetics: Rethinking Test-Time Scaling Laws**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.05333) — the abstract: once memory access is counted, the effectiveness of small models is overestimated, and under test-time scaling attention is the dominant cost (cited in W7; continues in W11)
- Łańcucki et al., **Inference-Time Hyper-Scaling with KV Cache Compression**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.05345) — the abstract: generation cost is bottlenecked by the size of the KV cache; compressing it buys more test-time tokens
- Mirtaheri et al., **Let Me Think! A Long Chain-of-Thought Can Be Worth Exponentially Many Short Ones**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.21825) — the abstract: there are reasoning problems (graph connectivity) where sequential scaling has an exponential advantage over parallel scaling
- Roberts et al., **Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal**, COLM 2026 (arXiv:2604.01411) — W7's $T^2$ law: the number of samples enters the training budget

**The dispute: does RL give a model new abilities?**
- Yue et al., **Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?**, NeurIPS 2025, oral (arXiv:2504.13837) — **assigned reading this week (in full)**; the abstract: RLVR-trained models win at small $k$, base models reach a higher pass@$k$ at large $k$; distillation can introduce new reasoning patterns
- Wen et al., **Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Implicitly Incentivizes Correct Reasoning in Base LLMs**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2506.14245) — **assigned reading this week (§4)**; proposes CoT-Pass@K, which counts a sample only if both its reasoning and its answer are correct; the abstract: under this metric RLVR extends the boundary
- Yuan et al., **Understanding Diversity Collapse in RLVR via the Lens of Overtraining**, arXiv:2606.15455 (2026) — the abstract: with few rollouts per problem, one observed success already saturates a problem's contribution to pass@$k$ at large $k$, so most updates in standard RLVR push that metric down by construction; **preprint**
- Yang, **When Pass@$k$ Crossovers Are Real — and Why: Paired Inference and the Markov Kernel of RLVR**, arXiv:2609.22547 (2026) — the abstract: neighbouring values of $k$ reuse samples, so a crossover needs paired inference; of nine public checkpoints only one narrowly passes, and truncation can create or hide a crossover; **preprint**
- Liu et al., **ProRL: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.24864) — the abstract: with long enough training, RL-trained models beat their base models across pass@$k$
- Yuan et al., **From $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ to $f(g(x))$: LLMs Learn New Skills in RL by Composing Old Ones**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2509.25123) — the abstract: on synthetic string functions, RL learns unseen compositions that next-token training on the same data does not
- Wu et al., **The Invisible Leash: Why RLVR May or May Not Escape Its Origin**, arXiv:2507.14843 (2025; a workshop paper, fifth version October 2026) — the abstract: matched question by question, more questions lose a verified success than gain one
- Matsutani et al., **RL Squeezes, SFT Expands: A Comparative Study of Reasoning LLMs**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2509.21128) — the abstract: RL compresses incorrect trajectories, SFT expands correct ones
- Wu et al., **Reasoning or Memorization? Unreliable Results of Reinforcement Learning Due to Data Contamination**, AAAI 2026 (arXiv:2507.10532) — last week's reading; the abstract: on clean generated problems only accurate rewards give steady gains beyond the base model's boundary

**Is the written reasoning the process? Faithfulness**
- Jacovi & Goldberg, **Towards Faithfully Interpretable NLP Systems: How should we define and evaluate faithfulness?**, ACL 2020 (arXiv:2004.03685) — where the term is defined
- Turpin et al., **Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.04388) — the origin of the hint paradigm
- Lanham et al., **Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning**, arXiv:2307.13702 (2023) — interventions on the chain of thought; **preprint**
- Chen et al., **Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think**, arXiv:2505.05410 (2025) — **the paper with the most teachable numbers**; the abstract: in most settings the hint is disclosed in fewer than 20% of cases; outcome-based RL raises the rate at first and then plateaus; **preprint**
- Chua & Evans, **Are DeepSeek R1 And Other Reasoning Models More Faithful?**, arXiv:2501.08156 (2025; a workshop paper) — the abstract: reasoning models describe the influence of a cue far more often than non-reasoning models
- Arcuschin et al., **Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2503.08679) — without any planted hint: coherent arguments for both of two contradictory answers
- Yu et al., **Outcome Rewards Do Not Guarantee Verifiable or Causally Important Reasoning**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2604.22074) — cited last week; the abstract: RLVR raises accuracy without reliably raising the causal importance or the sufficiency of the reasoning
- Boppana et al., **Reasoning Theater: Disentangling Model Beliefs from Chain-of-Thought**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2603.05488) — the abstract: on easy recall questions the answer can be decoded from activations long before the reasoning ends; on hard multi-hop questions the reasoning is genuine
- Zaman & Srivastava, **Is Chain-of-Thought Really Not Explainability? Chain-of-Thought Can Be Faithful without Hint Verbalization**, ACL 2026 (arXiv:2512.23032) — **the limits of the measurement**; the abstract: silence about a hint often reflects incompleteness, and larger inference budgets greatly increase verbalisation
- Emmons et al., **When Chain of Thought is Necessary, Language Models Struggle to Evade Monitors**, arXiv:2507.05246 (2025) — separates CoT as rationalisation from CoT as computation; **preprint**
- METR, **CoT May Be Highly Informative Despite "Unfaithfulness"**, a **blog post** by METR, 2025-08-08 (<https://metr.org/blog/2025-08-08-cot-may-be-highly-informative-despite-unfaithfulness/>) — **not peer-reviewed**; when the clue is too complex to use without writing the reasoning out, almost every trajectory shows it
- Gema et al., **Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Reasoning Models Varies with Where and How Preference Cues Are Delivered**, arXiv:2608.29464 (2026) — the abstract: across 15 open-weight models, cues that arrive in a tool return are verbalised less often than cues in the user message; **preprint**
- Lindsey et al., **On the Biology of a Large Language Model**, a research report from Anthropic (Transformer Circuits Thread, 2025-03-27, <https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html>) — **a company research report, not peer-reviewed**; the *Addition* section: internally the model uses two parallel pathways, yet when asked it describes the schoolbook carry algorithm

**Can we monitor a model through it? Monitorability**
- Korbak et al., **Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety**, arXiv:2507.11473 (2025) — **a position paper with no experiments**, by some forty authors
- Baker et al., **Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation**, arXiv:2503.11926 (2025) — the abstract: reading the CoT is an effective way to catch reward hacking; putting the monitor into the reward and optimising hard teaches the model to hide its intent; **preprint**
- Guan et al., **Monitoring Monitorability**, ICML 2026, spotlight (arXiv:2512.18311) — the abstract: most frontier models are fairly monitorable; longer reasoning is more monitorable; RL at the current scale does not materially reduce it
- Chen et al., **Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2603.05706) — the abstract: models control what their CoT says far less well than they control their final output
- Xiong, Chen & Lakkaraju, **Monitorability as a Free Gift: How RLVR Spontaneously Aligns Reasoning**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2602.03978) — the abstract: early RLVR sometimes raises monitorability as a side effect, but this depends strongly on the data and is unrelated to capability
- Little, **Length Penalties Make Chain-of-Thought Less Monitorable**, arXiv:2607.09786 (2026) — **the efficiency-versus-monitorability result**; for Qwen3-14B the monitor's catch rate falls from 71% to 51% (v4, §5), while a control without the length penalty shows no drop; **a single-author preprint**
- Wang et al., **MonitorBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in Large Language Models**, COLM 2026 (arXiv:2603.28590) — the abstract: monitorability is a conditional property, higher when the decisive factor has to pass through the reasoning

**Latent reasoning**
- Hao et al., **Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2412.06769) — Coconut: the last hidden state is fed back directly as the next input
- Zhu et al., **Reasoning by Superposition: A Theoretical Perspective on Chain of Continuous Thought**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.12514) — why continuous thoughts need fewer steps than discrete ones on graph reachability
- Yerram, He & Choi, **Training Continuous Chain of Thought Models: A Tale of Two Regimes**, arXiv:2607.16972 (2026; **a workshop paper**) — the abstract: on traces of a few hundred tokens or more, both training approaches lose roughly 65% of their performance
- Zou, Xiong & Liu, **Capabilities and Fundamental Limits of Latent Chain-of-Thought**, arXiv:2602.01148 (2026) — the abstract: good at exploration, poor at exact computation; **preprint**
- Wang et al., **Towards Inference-time Scaling for Continuous Space Reasoning**, Findings of ACL 2026 (arXiv:2510.12167) — the abstract: sampling shows headroom, but process and outcome reward models cannot tell correct from incorrect continuous reasoning
- Zhu et al., **A Survey on Latent Reasoning**, arXiv:2507.06203 (2025) — a map of the area; **preprint**

**The language a model reasons in**
- Tam et al., **Language Matters: How Do Multilingual Input and Reasoning Paths Affect Large Reasoning Models?**, arXiv:2505.17407 (2025) — the abstract: whatever the input language, reasoning tends to default to a high-resource language; **preprint**
- Qi et al., **When Models Reason in Your Language: Controlling Thinking Language Comes at the Cost of Accuracy**, Findings of EMNLP 2025 (arXiv:2505.22888) — the abstract: forcing the model to reason in the user's language improves readability and lowers accuracy
- Resck et al., **The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls**, arXiv:2610.22841 (2026) — the abstract: on parallel questions in eight languages, models rely more on their reasoning in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks; **preprint**

**Surveys**
- Chen et al., **Towards Reasoning Era: A Survey of Long Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Large Language Models**, arXiv:2503.09567 (2025) — a map of the area; **preprint**
- Zhang et al., **A Survey of Reinforcement Learning for Large Reasoning Models**, arXiv:2509.08827 (2025) — cited last week; **preprint**
